title: Chapter 4: Seven Shades in Chalk
blurb: After a night in the drain, Sorrel and Joan chalk out a plan for the Seven while a gale warning settles over Saturday's match.

blocks.text: The water in the dyke was black and very still, so still that the stars lay on it without shivering, and a thin rind of ice had grown along its margin, fine as the skin on cooling milk. Somewhere out on the levels a curlew called, the long rising call that sounds like a question asked of nobody, and then called again. I was knee-deep in a drainage dyke at three in the morning. I knew it was three because Hobsmere church struck it across the mere.

Someone's arms were locked round my chest. Someone was swearing, low and steady, about silt and back-flow and a sump that wanted digging out, the way you talk to a frightened animal so that it has a voice to hold on to and not the words.
It was Joan. And Joan was shaking so hard that I could hear her teeth.
"Joan," I said.
The swearing stopped. "There she is," Joan said into the back of my neck. "There she is. You're not going anywhere, are you?"

The line was still in me. It ran out of my chest across the far bank of the dyke, through the reed and over the mere and away into the dark toward Wenlode, where the Mallow birds would be on their perches by now with their heads under their wings, and every part of me that was not listening to Joan leaned along it. Joan leaned the other way. Between us we stood still.

I remembered the reed after Lucas let go, every stem edged with frost, and then I remembered nothing in any order I could trust. Joan told me the rest in pieces, through her teeth. She had followed us out from the Dyke Arms because she did not like the way Lucas held my hand. She had seen me go down the bank into the Back Drain, which runs behind the reed and out under it into the mere, and she had gone in after me, she who stood at the edge of that same water a week before with her arms out and did not go in. Twice Rhys and Abel had tried to lift us both up the near bank. Twice I had fought them toward the far side, where the drain opens to the mere, and the frozen clay had put all three of them back in the water. So Abel had tied a rope from Joan's belt to the alder on the bank, and Joan had put her back against the clay and her arms round me, and said, well, we'll stop here, then, won't we.
Only a tether can walk a Wing down. Anyone may hold her. So they held me.
A storm lantern stood on the bank above us, turned low, and beside it Rhys sat in his shirtsleeves with his knees drawn up. His coat was round my shoulders, and Abel's round Joan's.
"Morning, Crate," Rhys said. "You've had my good coat since eight o'clock. It'll never hang right again."
"Thank you for your coat, Rhys," I said, and I meant it, and he looked away and turned the lantern down a little further.
"Where's Lucas?"
Nobody answered. Then Abel said, "Up the causeway," and Joan said, "He'll come back, won't he," and that was all.

So we waited for the light. I put my hands over Joan's where they were locked at my breastbone, because her fingers were white and I could feel how cold they had gone, and I held them the way I would hold a bird that had come down chilled in the yard, not tight, only covering, so that whatever warmth I had could go into them. The stars went round over the mere. The curlew called and gave up calling. The ice crept out from the margin a finger's width at a time, and once a water rail screamed in the reed behind us and Joan's arms went hard as rope and then slowly soft again.
Held there, in the black water with the line pulling, I thought of something I had not thought of in years, and I did not say it.

When I was eleven I found a copper pigeon ring in the lane behind my aunt's house and closed it round my wrist for a bangle. That winter I saw a bird above me that went where I went, and I thought every child had one. And one evening a flock came over the fen, and there was one bird in it more than there should have been, and I walked after it. I walked two days. I never reached the flock, and nobody held my hand, and nobody walked me down, and on the second evening I turned round and came home on my own. My aunt said I had been sleepwalking. I let that be the story, because it was easier than any other. I knew now what the rules said about a Wing who walks after a flock with no tether, and I knew that they did not say what had happened to me.
This was not the first time I had walked after that bird.

The light came grey, then pale, then the colour of a pigeon's breast low over the levels, and out of Pollard's reed across the water the roost went up. I had never seen the outflight from so low. They rose in their thousands, in long, smoking ribbons that thickened and thinned and poured away east over the fields to feed, and the sound of their wings came over the water like rain beginning, and the whole sky was moving.
Lucas came down the causeway in it. His face was white as the ice. He did not say anything. He climbed down the bank into the water, which came above his knees, and took my hand, and began.
"One," he said.

It was fourteen minutes. He walked me up the drain and back, slowly, the three of us in the water, his hand in mine and Joan's arms never leaving me, and he talked about the mainspring of a carriage clock he was mending for the doctor's widow, and he counted. He did not look at the mere once. He kept his eyes on my face, or on the water at our feet, and his hand did not shake. At fourteen the line went out of my chest the way a tide goes out of a channel, all at once and quietly, and I was only a girl standing in a cold dyke at dawn with two people holding on to her.

On the bank, in Rhys's coat, I could not stop shivering, and Joan, soaked to the knee, could not stop either. She sat on the frozen grass with her boots full of water and looked at the drain, not at us.
"I can't swim," she said.
Nobody said anything. The last of the starlings went over.
"Never could. Silt engineer who can't swim. Lovely, isn't it." She pushed her wet hair off her face with the back of her wrist. "So I'm taking your withy on Saturday. Aren't I."
It was not a question. She had already answered it.

I looked at Lucas. He was standing a little apart, with his scarred hand closed at his side, and I waited for him to say that he was her tether, that it was his place, that he would do better. He did not argue. He only nodded, once, as if a thing had been taken off him that he had known for a long time he ought not to carry. I would have found it easier if he had argued, and I think so would he.
"Thank you, Joan," I said.
"Don't," she said. "Don't thank me. Get me some dry socks."
On Monday we told Pollard.

He met us at the far end of the causeway, on his own side, in a wind that had come round in the night and smelt of the sea, and Joan told it plainly, the drain and the rope and the alder and the dawn. Pollard listened with his hands in his coat. When she had finished he did not speak. A heron came over, very slow, and let down its legs into the reed by the feed shed. A long time went by. He took the chalk from his pocket and marked the gatepost beside him without looking at it, and then he looked at me.
"You've no second Wing," he said.
"No."
"Your rings are yours. Till they're cut." He was quiet. "Or till you speak one."
"Speak it to whom?"

"Another Wing. Say the number to her, and it's hers. She raises it as if she'd closed it herself. Hers till it's cut. Or handed back." He looked away over the reed toward the mere. "That's how a reserve comes on. If you go off. If you can't..."
"If I can't come back to the field," I said, "and there's someone to take them, the side still flies."
He nodded. "And it goes the other way."
"Someone could speak a number to me."
He did not answer that. He turned and walked toward the barn, and after a while we understood we were meant to follow.
The barn floor was beaten earth swept hard, and Pollard gave me his chalk.

We worked it out on our knees, Joan and I, while the wind went over the thatch. I drew the point bird first, small, and round it the seven things it watches. Six I could give it. At Mallow I had given it six, and the bird had turned for three wingbeats and its fellows had pulled it back, because six turns and only seven holds. Seven shades nearer the bird than any real bird, and to put seven shades round one bird you need seven ringed people within a pace of each other on the ground. We had six.
"So the seventh is theirs," Joan said.
"It has to be raised, at my ceiling, in the cluster."

Joan sat back on her heels. She had copied Wenlode's pages out of the flight book at the Loft the Friday before, after the Mallow draw, in pencil, and she unfolded them now on the floor. Every match Wenlode had flown this season, the counters' notes said the same: their Tackers marked the other side's Callers, a pace off, shade on shade.

"They mark at the Wing's ceiling," I said. "That's what marking is for. Gosmoor did it to me all match." I thought of how my shades had lagged and come apart, every change a breath too late, and something turned over in me that was very nearly gladness. "Their Tacker's shade will be up, and at my height, and wherever you go he goes."
"So I walk into our cluster," Joan said slowly, "and he follows me in, like a good dog. Doesn't he."

I drew him in, the seventh, a little apart from the six, then close. For a moment we both looked at it without speaking: seven marks in chalk round one small bird, on a barn floor, with the light going.
"Seven," Joan said.
In the doorway Pollard stood with his back to us, watching the sky. "Wind's going round," he said, and nothing else.

On Tuesday the wireless gave a gale for Saturday, severe, and Joan wrote that night to the Loft Court at Wenlode asking that the fixture be put back a week. The answer was waiting at the Dyke Arms on Thursday, in a long cream envelope, and Joan read it out at the bar in a flat voice.

"The Clerk of the Loft Court acknowledges the letter of Hobsmere Cutters dated Tuesday of this week. The Court notes that the rules as written provide that 'wild hawks, wind, fog, rain, frost, wild birds joining the flock, and tide or flood on coastal Reedbeds are part of the game, not fouls, unless a side caused them.' The Court notes further that no side has caused the wind. Mid-season the Court may rule only on whether something broke the rules as written. Nothing has. The request is refused. The fixture Wenlode Sluice versus Hobsmere Cutters stands for Saturday, the fifteenth matchday of Season CCIII. Given at the Ringing House, Wenlode. A. Stannard, Clerk."
The hand was upright and unhurried, every letter finished.
"She's quoted the weather at us," Rhys said. "Framed it and hung it up."
Joan folded the letter along its creases and put it in her pocket. "Well, that's the sump full," she said, "and the pump on the other side of the county, isn't it."
On Friday at noon I stood in the yard of the Circuit Loft, on the public side of the rail.

I had come in through that gate every morning for three winters with a feed pail in each hand. Now I stood among the club secretaries in their good coats and the wireless man with his notebook, and behind me, through the loft wall, I could hear the birds. I knew them by their voices. Mallow, low and sleepy, wanting their perches already though it was only noon. Sedgeway, who come easily to the hand. Tenpenny, quarrelsome over the water. And under all of them, high and quick and never still, the soft bickering of Cold Fleet, who go to pieces in any wind at all. The boy who has my job came out with a pail and went in again. He did not know me.

The wind was getting up. The weathercock on the loft roof had swung round in the night and would not rest, and the ribbons on the draw board lifted and fell. Five fixture cards hung there, each on its ribbon of club colours, and the loft-master stood beside them with the bag of flock tokens, the same felt bag, worn shiny at the neck, that I had held for him every Friday for three winters.
Joan came and stood beside me. She did not speak.

He drew four. Four tokens, four names read out, four cards with a flock tag hung on their ribbons, and the secretaries wrote them down and the wireless man wrote them down, and I heard none of them, because ours was the last card and I was listening to the loft behind me.
He put his hand in the bag. He drew the token and read it, and looked up at the board, and hung the tag on the last ribbon.
"Cold Fleet," he said. "Wenlode Sluice and Hobsmere Cutters."

The skittish flock, the one that had never once, in the flight book or in my three winters of feeding it, been settled in wind. Tonight it would go a few hundred yards down the hill in its crates to the Sluice Reedbed, and tomorrow, at the Loose, it would open into the gale.
